title: Seed and Offspring
english: "Let him stand with me." And concerning him the Savior says: 'There are some standing here who shall never taste death' (Matt 16:28).28).). Thus also Job had a house, which the wise man, "having built," established firmly "upon the rock" (Matt 7:24). Having this, even the disciples of Christ held an immovable stance, observing the life-saving words.

And "the house" of the intellect brings peace, being unmixed and unyielding, working the peace of virtue because it follows them; for nothing is discordant in the important matter. Concerning the virtues, the proverb is aptly spoken: 'Wise women built a house, but the foolish one dug it down with her hands' (Prov 14:1).wickedness works a distortion of the buildings quickly.

One virtue toward the building of a house is not sufficient. For this reason it is said in the plural: "Women built a house." But one wickedness is sufficient for distortion. For it is said: if anyone performs all the righteous acts, but performs one lawlessness, all his righteous deeds are set aside. For they no longer stand, nor do they remain, upon one [wrong] entering.

And his own virtue happens to be "not even to complain about the conduct of his tent" (Ps 119:10). For it is necessary for one progressing, which is shown through the tent, not to stumble nor to sin; for it is possible, even while one is still progressing, that the one dwelling in the house is already bringing peace through perfection, from the progressing of the one having borne fruit and singing: "I will pass through a place of tent-dwelling until the house of God" (Ps 119:154), in which the one having fallen short of having arrived at the perfection of virtue is slow-moving and most certain.

This is shown from: "Everyone born of God does not commit sin" (1 John 3:9). And assigning the cause, he asserts: "because his seed remains in him," saying that [it] made him. For concerning such a thing it is also said in the Gospel: "No one is able to snatch [them] out of the hand of my Father" (John 10:28). And we did not say that the virtuous one is unshakeable, but that he is difficult to shake.

But by himself he would become outside the hand of God by falling away; for "they themselves" say "they pushed [him] out from your hand" (Matt 26:56), clearly having become unworthy of being guarded by the hand of God, which Judas himself experienced, going out from the covering hand of God. For he has not said...

No one will come out, but 'no one is able to snatch [them] from the hand of my Father' (John 10:28). He himself will reject those who previously tore themselves away. For it is said: 'God will strike them down, because they did not listen to him' (Ps 67:4), the one who guards, knowing that his seed is very much. For the earth of the diligent mind is good, receiving the seeds from the Word of the Brideway [the Bridegroom] familiarly and eagerly, or he himself sows the disciples through the Word given to him.

And the seed is often called a child: 'the seed of Abraham'—his children—not necessarily being both seed and child already. Regarding the Jews who cry out that they are the seed of Abraham, the Savior did not say: 'You lie,' but led forward: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham (John 8:39); for not all these [are] from Israel, the [descendants] of Israel. Nor is it that they are the seed of Abraham always a child.' He therefore says to them as not being children of Abraham: 'Do the desires of your father.' But those doing the desires of the devil, accepting him as father, are not children of Abraham. Blessed is the one becoming the seed of Abraham according to having the virtues of godliness and becoming a child, through being formed and not becoming dull, but bringing forth.

And there is when both the seed and the child are said in parallel, as is also set forth in the present. The intellect of the holy, which must be understood, brings forth offspring corresponding to the 'increase of the field' and a multitude exceeding in vital power, so that this 'man of the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 13:47) might thus 'become like' according to the Gospel, sowing in the field of his own heart, so that he might bear fruit 'a hundred, sixty, thirty' (Matt 13:8) at first, middle, and last, 'sowing in tears' (Ps 126:5), so that 'he may reap in joy' (Ps 126:6) and 'seeking the Lord, so that he may bring to him fruits of righteousness.' 'He will be released in a tomb like grain ripe being harvested in season, or like wheat of a threshing floor being gathered according to the hour.' Nothing of the existing things is without a proper end, even if it is taken by art. Nature and art both have an end and a purpose; for a vine is grown for the reasonable enjoyment of man, and a house is built by a craftsman having a purpose to complete a house for habitation. title: Virtue and Purpose
english: The creation of humanity is rooted in the idea that people were created to live a life of virtue, as it is said, 'The word became flesh, man was created, to live according to virtue.' This concept is echoed in Psalm 39:4, where the psalmist prays, 'Make me know my end and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what I lack,' demonstrating a desire to understand one's mortality and the limited time available to live a virtuous life (Psalm 39:4). The psalmist's prayer implies that he was created to live according to virtue and to participate in God's wisdom, speaking and acting in accordance with it. However, he acknowledges that he falls short in many areas, which he attributes to his own limitations, and so he asks God to reveal to him the end of his life, that he may know how much time he has left to make up for his deficiencies. The book of Ecclesiastes also touches on this idea, warning that one should not be hard, lest they die not in their time, as stated in Ecclesiastes 7:17, which serves as a warning to not neglect the pursuit of virtue, lest one's life be cut short before reaching its full potential. Similarly, David prays in Psalm 102:24, 'Do not take me away in the midst of my days,' expressing his desire to live a full and complete life (Psalm 102:24). Abraham, on the other hand, is described as 'old and full of days,' which is not merely a reference to his advanced age, but rather an indication of his spiritual maturity and fulfillment, having lived a life that was full and complete. The concept of being 'full of days' is not just about living a long life, but about receiving the illuminations of 'the sun of righteousness' without interruption, and being honored with the presbeia, or spiritual eldership, that comes from living a life of wisdom and virtue, as stated in Wisdom of Solomon 4:8-9, 'For old age is not measured by the number of years, but by the grayness of wisdom, and old age is a life without turmoil' (Wisdom of Solomon 4:8-9). Since Abraham believed in God and his faith was reckoned as righteousness, and he was 'full of days' and 'old,' it is fitting that he died in good old age, having lived a life that was full and complete. The fullness of days is understood in this way and is confirmed from other sources, such as the commandment to 'Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the Lord your God is giving you' (Exodus 20:12, Deuteronomy 5:16). However, this is not an absolute guarantee, as many who have shown great honor to their parents have died prematurely, while others who have dishonored their mothers and fathers have lived long lives. Additionally, in Psalm 91:16, it is written concerning the one who dwells in the help of the Most High, 'With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation,' which indicates completion and fulfillment, rather than merely a long life (Psalm 91:16). For it is said that one is snatched away, so that evil may not change his understanding, as stated in Psalm 91. All these things are said to us to show that events occur for a certain purpose and from many, but much more from God. Elihu, knowing this, says that the one who receives admonition gently and toward a return will have a good and honorable end, which is indicated to him by the fact that 'he will come into the grave like ripe wheat harvested in season' (Job 5:26). The word of God follows him in sequence, saying, 'Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves' (Psalm 94:12), when he is also exhorted not to despise the admonition of the Almighty, as He strikes and wounds, yet saves him from six distresses, from the sword, and from the famine and war, and from the scourge of the tongue, and from the hiding of iron. On all these things, Elihu says, a good end will be received in due time and season, just as grain is gathered in a threshing floor. And it is blessed to be such grain, about which the Savior says, 'The good seed are the children of the kingdom' (Matthew 13:38). The Savior also teaches that 'unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a single seed. But if it dies, it produces many seeds' (John 12:24), which means that the fruit of this grain is not merely physical offspring, but rather people who are the children of the kingdom. It is a great thing not to hear the words, 'I will pull you up and transplant you from your dwelling and your root from the land of the living' (Jeremiah 22:28), but rather to be filled with virtues like the grain that is filled and harvested in due time and season. The time and the hour are laid down in parallel, as in the command to 'Keep this law at the appointed times' (Exodus 12:2, Exodus 13:10). The spiritual perfection of the soul is not unripe, for it is written that 'those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy' (Psalm 126:5), which shows the beginning of virtue through their labors and exercises; but 'those who go out weeping, carrying their seeds, will return with songs of joy, carrying their sheaves' (Psalm 126:6), which signifies perfection and fulfillment. For the perfect one is indeed on a firm foundation, and we learn this well from the Savior, who teaches us about the importance of living a virtuous life and receiving the illuminations of the sun of righteousness…

title: Job's Magnanimity and the Nature of His Suffering
english: He cleanses his threshing floor and gathers the grain into a granary, and burns the chaff with a lime-fire. It is clear that these things are not spoken concerning sensible things; for chaff is not burned with a lime-fire, nor does he seem to take up threshing concerning a sensible woman—for man is not a threshing-woman—but rather the perfection and fullness, as we have said.

We have, most wisely, in the Song of Songs, something said concerning the bride, who is the church or the perfected soul: 'Your navel is like a rounded vessel; the swelling of your womb is like a fenced threshing-floor of lilies' (Song of Songs 4:2). And that the soul does not have this commonly called 'belly,' concerning which it is said: 'food for the belly and the belly for food' (1 Corinthians 6:13), but rather that one concerning which it is written: 'your law in the midst of my belly' (Psalm 119:11), and: 'from the fear of you in the belly we have endured pain and have given birth' (Isaiah 42:14).

And this same soul also has a 'navel' which is the middle of the intellect, which has become, according to the 'wine having been strained by wisdom,' the divine thoughts and having ascended super-eminently. And since these things were not able to be thought by men, they were strained with human words, so that in this way they might reach the 'swelling,' to receive the hearing of the naked, those unable to [hear] the things of wisdom.

And it is possible to show the non-human through the vessel, but also to say to the [human]: that you have an old and new scripture, which is the vessel, in the middle of your ruling principle. And you also have a 'belly' resembling a threshing-floor, 'fenced in lilies.' For since the lily has white on the outside, but a dark color inside, it would perhaps show that the perfected soul becomes white according to the word, concerning which it was said: 'my sister is white' (Song of Songs 6:4), being killed from the deathfulness of asceticism.

'Behold, these things we have searched out, these are the things we have heard. But you, know yourself if you have done anything' (Job 28:24). The aforementioned is confirmed, that being wise and perhaps having heard from old saints who taught divinely without writing, he was led to say someone having a reason, of which we also find similar things in the divine letters and set them aside. For through 'we have searched out' his wisdom is demonstrated, and through 'we have heard'...

Unless someone says that he speaks of instruction as if it were experience and knowledge of things, he follows the same beginning and remains [with the idea] that he has suffered through sin, and he brought forward: 'But know yourself if you have done anything,' so that he might also through this be making it manifest that: [gap] what I said concerning those committing sin; for I do not think it just to be punished. But I do not know the [details] of each of the sins.

'But know yourself,' which is to say: having known, repent, which is again remaining as if he were concerning a sin. For he thought one cause for the inductions. 'And having understood, Job says: If indeed anyone were to set my anger in a yoke, and to lift my pains in a yoke together, and indeed it would be heavier than a sandbank.' Just as from all the other things, so also from the things set forth, the magnanimity of Job is shown, bearing the circumstances bravely and very manfully. For many, when they come into circumstantial and distressing [situations], they consider those who exhort and [gap] blame them as superfluous. But this one has prepared himself even for an answer [gap] of the circumstances [gap].

Therefore, he would say the things set forth against the things spoken by Eliphaz: 'But now toil has come upon you and has touched you, and you have hurried' (Job 2:10), to demonstrate at the same time that these things are not happening because of sins, and [to show] moderation, supposing himself to be wavering even though the inspired spirit of the writer testifies to him that he might be 'blameless.' Therefore he says: if anyone would desire to set our trespasses and the provoked anger in a yoke, he would find it heavier than our trespasses. For the saint knew that these things were not happening because of sins but because of a struggle, where in the following he declared: 'I know that I shall appear righteous' (Job 27:6). Therefore he strove to lead his friends into such knowledge.

And if even the 'setting' signifies the cessation, he perceived it. And let it be understood thus: a yoke is said to be lying upon the neck of suffering animals. He might be saying: if anyone would be willing to pull with me the yoke of sufferings, so as to silence me from them through fellowship.
